slides.0.title: Brands, marketing and consumers
slides.0.subtitle: Consumers buy not just wine but trust and story
slides.1.title: Brands and regions
slides.1.highlights.0.title: What brands do
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Brands reduce the consumer’s search cost and guarantee consistent style year after year; big brands keep consistency through cross-regional blending and scale (Champagne NV, big Australian brands)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Appellations are brands too
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Names such as Champagne, Prosecco and Rioja are collective brands promoted by trade bodies and protected by law; protecting a name (e.g. South African “Port” relabelled as Cape styles from 2012) protects brand value
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The two sides of national image
slides.1.highlights.2.content: A “good value” image helps volume but makes premium bottles hard to sell (Chile, South Africa); conversely, a prestige image helps entry-level wines sell (regional Bordeaux and Burgundy)
slides.1.content: Brands and appellations are two sources of trust: one relies on a company, the other on a system.
slides.2.title: Scores, media and packaging
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Scores and critics
slides.2.highlights.0.content: High scores can push demand and prices up quickly, especially in en primeur; critics argue scores favoured rich styles and pushed many regions towards high ripeness and heavy oak in the 1990s–2000s
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Digital and social media
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Online retail, social media and wine-rating apps let small wineries reach consumers directly and spread word of mouth faster, but information overload also makes brands harder to remember
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Packaging innovation
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Screwcaps, bag-in-box, cans and lightweight glass cut cost and carbon; but in traditional markets glass and cork still signal quality, so acceptance varies by market
slides.2.content: Every marketing tool has side effects: scores raise prices but homogenise style; light packaging saves carbon but may look cheap.
slides.3.title: Consumer trends
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Falling consumption
slides.3.highlights.0.content: OIV data show global wine consumption in 2025 at its lowest since 1961 (about 214 million hl); health awareness, changing habits among younger drinkers and economic pressure are common explanations
slides.3.highlights.1.title: “Drink less but better”
slides.3.highlights.1.content: As total volume falls, mid-to-premium and distinctive wines hold up relatively well, a trend called premiumisation; cheap bulk and commodity wine are hit hardest
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Low and no alcohol, and sustainability
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Low- and no-alcohol categories are growing, and organic, sustainability certification and lightweight glass are key messages; but “sustainable” claims without certification are easily challenged as greenwashing
slides.3.content: Split trend questions into volume and mix: volume is falling, but the mix is moving upmarket.

A. Volume wines will not sell

What effect of scores is most often criticised?
A. Pushing styles towards rich, oaky homogeneity

A. A rising share of bulk
C. Mid-to-premium wines holding up as total volume falls
D. All wines rising in price together
